1.q: דְּבַר־יְהוָ֣ה ׀ אֲשֶׁ֣ר הָיָ֗ה אֶל־מִיכָה֙ הַ⁠מֹּ֣רַשְׁתִּ֔י בִּ⁠ימֵ֥י יוֹתָ֛ם אָחָ֥ז יְחִזְקִיָּ֖ה מַלְכֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה אֲשֶׁר־חָזָ֥ה עַל־שֹׁמְר֖וֹן וִ⁠ירֽוּשָׁלִָֽם
1.note: Micah is speaking of himself in the third person as **Micah** and **he** to introduce this book.
The pronoun **he** refers to Micah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which Micah saw]

Micah is using the possessive form to describe a **word** that comes from **Yahweh**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The word from Yahweh]

2.note: Micah is speaking to the **earth**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the judgment that Yahweh is about to bring. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the earth. Alternate translation: [everyone on earth should pay attention]

Here, **its fullness** represents everything and everyone that fills the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [earth, and everything and everyone in it]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from his holy palace]

3.note: Micah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Pay attention for]

Micah is speaking of Yahweh acting with power over the earth as if he would **tread on the high places of the earth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act with power over even the highest places of the earth]

4.note: Micah is speaking of the effect of Yahweh’s powerful presence as if the solid **mountains will melt under him**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And it will be like the mountains will soften and flow out from beneath him]

4.q: וְ⁠הָ⁠עֲמָקִ֖ים יִתְבַּקָּ֑עוּ כַּ⁠דּוֹנַג֙ מִ⁠פְּנֵ֣י הָ⁠אֵ֔שׁ כְּ⁠מַ֖יִם מֻגָּרִ֥ים בְּ⁠מוֹרָֽד
4.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the comparisons of the wax and the water with the information about the mountains melting as modeled in the UST.

The point of this comparison is that just as **wax** melts when it is near a **fire**, so it will be as if the mountains will melt away because of the power of Yahweh’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as wax melts when it is near a fire]

Micah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [melts because of the heat of the fire]

The point of this comparison is that just as **waters** rush swiftly and unstoppably down a **steep place**, so the will the mountains quickly melt before the powerful presence of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as swiftly and unstoppably as waters rushing down a steep place]

The expression **poured** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like waters that pour down from a steep place]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgression**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of how Jacob has rebelled]

Here Micah is using the name **Jacob** to refer to the people of Israel who were all descendants of the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

Micah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Samaria is the cause of Jacob’s transgression!]

Micah is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And Jerusalem lead Judah to worship idols on the high places!]

6.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh said, “So I will make”]

The pronoun **her** refers to the city of Samaria, which Yahweh speaks of as if it were a woman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Samaria’s stones into the gorge, and Samaria’s foundations]

7.note: The expression **crushed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And enemies will crush all Samaria’s carved images]

The expression **burned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and fire will burn up all her wages]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will completely destroy]
The pronoun **they** refers to the idols and treasures that Samaria gathered. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these treasures will be used again]

8.note: The terms **lament** and **wail** mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I shall greatly mourn]

Going about without sandals or clothing was a symbolic action by which Micah showed his deep grief and mourning over the coming disaster. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I shall go barefoot and naked to show my grief]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the jackals** make loud, wailing cries, so Micah’s **lamentation** will be loud and mournful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I shall make a lamentation as loud and mournful as the cries of the jackals]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lamentation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mournful wailing]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the daughters of an owl** make mournful, crying sounds, so Micah’s **mourning** will sound. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and mourning that sounds like the crying of young owls]

Micah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I shall make mourning like the daughters of an owl]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mourning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I shall mourn]

9.note: Micah is speaking of the destruction that has struck the city as if it were **wounds** that cannot be healed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the destruction that struck her cannot be undone]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wounds**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the places where she is wounded]

The pronoun **it** refers to the disaster and judgment that Yahweh is bringing. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for this disaster has also come to Judah. This disaster has reached]

Here, **gate** represents the city of Jerusalem itself, since the gate was the main entrance to the city and the place where it was defended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the city of my people]

10.note: The word translated as **declare** sounds like the name of the city, **Gath**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
The pronoun **it** refers to the news of the coming disaster. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [do not declare the news of the disaster]

Micah is repeating forms of the verb **weep** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [certainly you should not weep]
The name of the town **Beth Leaphrah** means “house of dust.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

Rolling oneself **in the dust** was a symbolic action by which a person showed deep grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [roll yourself in the dust to show your grief]

11.q: שָׁפִ֖יר עֶרְיָה־בֹ֑שֶׁת לֹ֤א יָֽצְאָה֙ יוֹשֶׁ֣בֶת צַֽאֲנָ֔ן מִסְפַּד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֵ֔צֶל יִקַּ֥ח מִ⁠כֶּ֖ם
11.note: The name of the town **Shaphir** means “pleasant” or “beautiful,” the opposite of **nakedness** and **shame**. The name of the town **Zaanan** sounds like the verb “go out.” The name of the town **Beth Ezel** may mean “house of taking away.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [shamefully naked]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **mourning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when the people of Beth Ezel mourn, it]
The pronoun **its** refers to the town of Beth Ezel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [will take from you the standing place of Beth Ezel]

12.note: The name of the town **Maroth** sounds like the word for “bitterness,” an opposite of **good.** If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

Micah is using the adjective **evil** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [terrible things have come down from Yahweh]

Here, **the gate** represents the city of Jerusalem itself, since the gate was its main entrance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to Jerusalem itself]

13.note: The name of the town **Lachish** sounds like the word for “steed.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

Even though Micah has addressed the people of Lachish directly as **dweller of Lachish**, here he speaks of them in the third person as **She** and then switches back to addressing them as **you**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this consistently in the second person. Alternate translation: [You were the beginning of sin]

Micah is speaking of the city of Zion, that is, Jerusalem, and its people as if they were his **daughter**. This form of expression conveys affection. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to my beloved people of Zion]

The expression **were found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for people found in you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgressions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sinful things that Israel did]

14.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [As a result,]

The town **Moresheth Gath** is Micah’s hometown. The part of the name **Moresheth** sounds like the word for “betrothed.” The idea is that, just as a father gave a gift of money (a dowry) along with his daughter to the man she married, the leaders of Jerusalem will have to give tribute to Assyria as they also give them their towns, such as Moresheth Gath.
The name of the town **Achzib** sounds like the word for “deception.” If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deception**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will turn out to be deceptive]

15.q: עֹ֗ד הַ⁠יֹּרֵשׁ֙ אָ֣בִי לָ֔⁠ךְ יוֹשֶׁ֖בֶת מָֽרֵשָׁ֑ה
15.note: The name of the town **Mareshah** sounds like the word for **possessor.** If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

Here, **glory** represents the honored, important leaders of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [honored ones of Israel]

By **The glory of Israel will come to Adullam**, Micah means that the honored leaders of Israel will go into hiding there, just as David once hid in the caves near Adullam to escape his enemies (described in 1 Samuel 22:1). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Israel’s honored leaders will flee to hide in the caves near Adullam, as David once did]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [The glorious ones of Israel]

16.note: The terms translated as **Make yourself bald** and **shave** mean similar things. Micah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Shave your head completely bald]

Shaving the head completely bald was a symbolic action by which the people would show their deep grief and mourning. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Make yourself bald and shave to show your grief]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes all children whether male or female. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women as modeled in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **delight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sons who delight you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the eagle** has a bare, featherless head, so the people are to make their **baldness** in mourning complete. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Make your baldness complete, so that your head is as bare as an eagle’s head]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **baldness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bald area on your head]
This word could mean: (1) an eagle, or (2) a vulture. Alternate translation: [like the vulture]

The pronoun **they** refers to the children whom Micah told the people to mourn for. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for your children have gone into exile from you]
